title: Silence fences wisdom (Avot 3:13)
hookLine: Akiva: tradition is a fence for Torah, tithes for wealth, vows for restraint, silence for wisdom
tomorrow: what's better than being loved? Akiva has an answer.

cards: A message typed in anger can sit in the box for a minute before it's sent, and that minute has saved a lot of friendships. Rabbi Akiva had a stranger kind of pause in mind.
In one breath he lists fences: tradition is a fence for the Torah, tithes are a fence for wealth, vows are a fence for self-restraint, and a fence for wisdom is silence. Here's the odd part.
A fence usually keeps you out of something. Why would anyone fence in the thing they want?

teach.b: Look at what the first fences protect. Tradition, masoret, the handed-down way of reading, guards the Torah from being bent into whatever a reader wishes.
Tithes guard wealth, which is a surprise: giving some away keeps the rest from owning you. Vows guard restraint: a promise made before the craving shows up.
So a fence in Avot isn't a wall against the good thing. It's a ring around the good thing, so it doesn't get trampled. Now the last one: seyag lachochmah shtikah, a fence for wisdom is silence.
Wisdom doesn't need protecting from other people.
It needs protecting from your own mouth: the hot take, the reply sent too soon, the clever line that costs a friend.
Silence keeps open the space where listening happens. Proverbs, in the King James wording, puts the side effect plainly: "Even a fool, when he holdeth his peace, is counted wise." Akiva goes further.
The quiet person isn't just thought wise; the quiet is how wisdom gets time to grow. And notice what he doesn't say: never speak. A fence has a gate.

how: Jewish ethical writing praises guarded speech; Avot 1:17 says nothing is better for the body than silence, and some Jews take on a pause before speaking in anger as a practice.

o: quiet guards what you know, like a fence
the wisest people never say a word

s: Akiva says the wise never speak
silence is the fence, and a fence has a gate.
in Akiva's list, tithes are a fence for wealth
giving some away guards the rest.
Proverbs says even a fool who holds his peace is counted wise
Proverbs 17:28, in the King James wording.

games.q: in a team meeting your boss asks who dropped the ball on a project. you know, and you're annoyed about it. by Akiva's fence, what first?
o: say nothing yet; listen, and speak once you know it helps.
name the person right away so the truth gets out.
make a joke about it to lighten the room.
games.why: silence is a fence, not a wall: it buys time to listen, and the gate still opens when speaking helps.

practice: Close your eyes and let the room go quiet. Each time a sentence starts forming, a reply, a comeback, a plan, notice it at the gate and let it wait outside. Two minutes of fence, with nothing to defend.

wordCard.voice: Silence fences wisdom. Akiva's seyag, a fence: quiet as the ring that keeps what you know from being trampled by what you say.

orig.note: Hebrew: a fence or hedge, the word Akiva uses for each guard in his list.

carryVoice: Carry this: silence fences wisdom, and the fence always has a gate for when words can help. Until tomorrow.
